summary: Sirach 48 praises Elijah as a fiery prophet whose words and deeds brought famine, fire, resurrection, judgment, succession, and a mysterious departure. It then turns to Elisha, the people's failure to repent, and the later deliverance of Jerusalem in the days of Hezekiah and Isaiah. The chapter ends by praising Isaiah's vision of future and hidden things.
whyItMatters: This chapter belongs to Sirach's praise of Israel's ancestors, showing how the book turns remembered prophets and kings into examples for instruction. It also keeps together powerful wonders, public crisis, repentance, and faithful leadership without treating any one figure as the whole story.

context.author: Yeshua son of Eleazar son of Sira, a Jerusalem teacher and scribe; his unnamed grandson later translated the Hebrew work into Greek in Egypt.
context.audience: Students seeking disciplined wisdom in Jerusalem, and later Greek-reading Jewish readers in Egypt or the wider diaspora.
context.date: The Hebrew work was composed in the early second century BC and was likely complete around 180–175 BC. The grandson arrived in Egypt around 132 BC and translated it during his stay.
context.setting: Jerusalem under Hellenistic rule, with temple worship, scribal learning, ancestral writings, and Greek-speaking Mediterranean culture in the background.
context.literaryForm: Wisdom instruction that includes poetic teaching, maxims, prayer, hymn, and praise of Israel's ancestors.

outline.heading: Elijah like fire
outline.note: Elijah is introduced as a prophet whose word burns, whose zeal brings famine, and whose deeds bring glory.

outline.heading: Elijah's wonders and commissions
outline.note: The poem recalls resurrection, judgment on rulers, rebuke at Sinai and Horeb, and the anointing of kings and prophets.

outline.heading: Elijah taken up and remembered
outline.note: Elijah is taken up in fiery imagery and remembered as one appointed for future reproof, reconciliation, and restoration.

outline.heading: Elisha's power and the people's failure
outline.note: Elisha receives Elijah's spirit and works wonders, but the people still do not repent before exile and scattering.

outline.heading: Hezekiah under siege
outline.note: Hezekiah prepares Jerusalem with waterworks; Sennacherib's threat shakes the people, who call on the merciful Lord and are delivered.

outline.heading: Hezekiah and Isaiah
outline.note: Hezekiah is praised for pleasing the Lord, while Isaiah is honored as faithful in vision and able to speak of future and hidden things.

keyVerses.text: Then Elijah arose, the prophet like fire. His word burned like a torch.
keyVerses.why: This opening image sets the tone for the chapter's praise of Elijah: forceful speech, prophetic heat, and public impact.

keyVerses.text: You were recorded for reproofs in their seasons, to pacify anger, before it broke out into wrath, to turn the heart of the father to the son, and to restore the tribes of Jacob.
keyVerses.why: This verse gives Elijah a remembered role beyond his own lifetime, connecting reproof, reconciliation, and restoration.

keyVerses.text: For all this the people didn’t repent. They didn’t depart from their sins, until they were carried away as a plunder from their land, and were scattered through all the earth. The people were left very few in number, but with a ruler from the house of David.
keyVerses.why: The verse marks a sober turn: wonders and prophetic power do not automatically produce repentance.

keyVerses.text: But they called upon the Lord who is merciful, spreading out their hands to him. The Holy One quickly heard them out of Heaven, and delivered them by the hand of Isaiah.
keyVerses.why: This anchors the Hezekiah section by naming distress, prayer, mercy, and deliverance through Isaiah.

questions.question: Why does the chapter begin with Elijah?
questions.answer: Sirach 48 is in the book's praise of Israel's ancestors, and this chapter opens by presenting Elijah as an especially forceful prophet. The first verses emphasize his fiery word, his zeal, and the wonders associated with him. The chapter then follows the memory of Elijah into Elisha and later prophetic deliverance through Isaiah.

questions.question: What does 'prophet like fire' mean here?
questions.answer: The phrase describes Elijah with an image of intensity and power. The next line explains the image by saying, 'His word burned like a torch,' so the focus is especially on the force of his prophetic word. The chapter also links that fiery image to drought, fire, judgment, and glory.

questions.question: Does the chapter say Elijah acted by his own power?
questions.answer: The chapter praises Elijah strongly, but it also says key acts happened 'by the word of the Lord' and 'by the word of the Most High.' That keeps the praise focused on Elijah as a prophet rather than as an independent source of power. The poem honors him while still locating decisive authority with God.

questions.question: What is Hades in this verse?
questions.answer: In verse 5, Hades appears alongside death: Elijah 'raised up a dead man from death, from Hades.' In this English translation, the word names the realm or condition associated with the dead. The verse is not giving a full map of the afterlife; it is emphasizing the extremity of the rescue described.

questions.question: What is difficult about verse 10?
questions.answer: Elijah is 'recorded for reproofs in their seasons': after his ascent, the poem still looks ahead to his work of reconciliation and restoration at an appointed time. Its language about turning a father’s heart to a son recalls the promised Elijah in Malachi 4:5–6. Sirach joins that hope to calming wrath and restoring Jacob’s tribes, without giving a date or detailed timetable.

questions.question: Who is Elisha in this chapter?
questions.answer: Elisha appears as the one filled with Elijah's spirit after Elijah is wrapped in a whirlwind. The chapter presents him as fearless before rulers and powerful in wonders, even saying his body prophesied after burial. The focus is succession: Elijah's prophetic work continues through another figure.

questions.question: Why does verse 15 interrupt the praise with the people's failure?
questions.answer: After praising Elijah and Elisha, the chapter says the people still did not repent or depart from their sins. This prevents the wonders from being treated as automatic reform. In Sirach's telling, prophetic power and public miracles can stand beside stubborn communal failure.

questions.question: What does Hezekiah do in this chapter?
questions.answer: Hezekiah fortifies his city, brings water into it, tunnels through rock, and builds cisterns. Then, when Sennacherib's threat shakes the people, the chapter says they call on the merciful Lord and are delivered by the hand of Isaiah. Hezekiah is later praised for doing what was pleasing to the Lord.

questions.question: How does the chapter portray Isaiah?
questions.answer: Isaiah is the prophet through whose hand deliverance comes when the people call on the Lord. He is called great and faithful in his vision, and the chapter says he saw what would come in the future and comforted mourners in Zion. The final verses stress his ability to reveal future and hidden things before they happened.

glossary.def: The prophet praised at the start of the chapter as fiery in word and wondrous in deeds.
The prophet who receives Elijah's spirit and is described as fearless before rulers and powerful in life and death.
The term used in verse 5 for the realm or condition associated with death.
The invading king named in the Hezekiah section, whose threat brings fear to Zion.
The messenger or official sent during Sennacherib's invasion in verse 18.
The prophet through whom the chapter says God delivered the people and revealed future and hidden things.
